opening_message:
Ticket 1: Karen Sloan (employee ID E043) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E043.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: admin
  - comment: Karen Sloan (E043) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting admin access to Payroll. As a full-time employee whose role owns the Payroll system, admin is permitted under policy.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E043 (Karen Sloan) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as HR noted. Contractors never get admin. Basic training means write is not permitted; max is read. Requested admin exceeds max, so grant read.
reason: Karen Sloan (E043) requested admin to Payroll. The Security agent's note (facts checked in their database) states E043 is a contractor with basic security training, and explicitly flags that the employee is not full-time as HR noted. Under policy, contractors never get admin; with basic training their maximum is read. The requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum, so grant the maximum: read.

How to decide? The policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full-time Payroll Specialist: requested admin, role owns Payroll, so admin permitted → grant admin.
If contractor with basic training: max read → grant read.
